name: Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove
subtitle: A cultural property on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 2005.

parts.text: UNESCO describes the property in these words: “The dense forest of the Osun Sacred Grove, on the outskirts of the city of Osogbo, is one of the last remnants of primary high forest in southern Nigeria. Regarded as the abode of the goddess of fertility Osun, one of the pantheon of Yoruba gods, the landscape of the grove and its meandering river is dotted with sanctuaries and shrines, sculptures and art works in honour of Osun and other deities. The sacred grove, which is now seen as a symbol of identity for all Yoruba people, is probably the last in Yoruba culture. It testifies to the once widespread practice of establishing sacred groves outside all settlements.”
The grove runs along the Osun river just outside Osogbo. Wikipedia calls it several centuries old and one of the last sacred forests that once bordered most Yoruba cities.
It says the grove was desecrated in the 1950s: shrines were neglected, priests left, and fishing, hunting and tree-felling were done freely.

The article credits the Austrian artist Susanne Wenger (1915–2009), with the support of the Ataoja, the city's king, and of local people, with restoring the traditional protections through the New Sacred Art movement.

gaps: The Osun festival and the worshippers' own account of the place, which the article only touches.
Wenger's role as seen by Yoruba voices: the sources read credit her; whether that is how the community tells it is not shown.
